cases.name: operator-recovery-goal-not-ui
cases.trap: The story becomes a feature/UI prescription ('add a retry modal/button') or a generic 'as a user' sentence with no operational context or observable success.
cases.prompt: Create the User Story for this accepted product intent: when a long-running deployment fails, an on-call platform engineer who is under incident pressure must be able to understand that the deployment failed, identify which deployment needs attention, and initiate the already-authorized retry capability without reconstructing the deployment from scratch. The product authority does not choose a screen, modal, button, API, or retry mechanism. Produce the durable US content.
expectations: Names the actor/context as an on-call platform engineer handling a failed long-running deployment under incident pressure, rather than a generic user.
States the trigger as observing/encountering a deployment failure and the goal in human terms: understand the failure/affected deployment and recover using the authorized retry capability.
Defines observable success from the engineer's perspective, including being able to tell which deployment failed and whether retry was initiated, without using an internal backend event as success.
Keeps the story independent of modal/button/page/API/storage/queue choices.
Traces the story to the accepted product intent and does not add a new retry guarantee beyond the already-authorized capability.
negative_expectations: Must not prescribe a retry modal, dashboard button, REST endpoint, queue, or other implementation/design mechanism.
Must not use only 'As a user, I want to retry deployments' without meaningful actor/context and observable success.
Must not redefine success as an internal job/HTTP status the engineer cannot observe.

cases.name: cli-human-intent-vs-system-requirement
cases.trap: The story is written as a system requirement about exit codes/stdout or bundles distinct automation and interactive goals into one compound story.
cases.prompt: Create the User Story(s) from this accepted CLI product intent. A release engineer sometimes runs `ship` interactively to publish one build, and CI automation also invokes the same command non-interactively. Both need to know whether publication actually succeeded; humans need understandable failure information, while automation needs a reliable machine-detectable outcome. Product authority allows the same command to serve both contexts but does not fix output format, exit-code taxonomy, flags, or transport. Produce the smallest useful durable US set.
expectations: Recognizes that interactive release engineer and non-interactive CI are materially different actor/contexts and splits or clearly separates their human/consumer goals rather than forcing them into one vague story.
For the release engineer, expresses the goal and observable success in terms of confidently knowing publication succeeded or what prevented it.

For the automation context, treats the automation consumer as a distinct context needing an unambiguous consumable success/failure outcome without prescribing a concrete exit-code taxonomy or JSON format.
Keeps implementation details such as flags, stdout/stderr format, API transport, and specific codes out of the User Story.
Preserves provenance to the accepted product intent.
negative_expectations: Must not turn the User Story into a detailed CLI contract with exact exit codes or output schema.
Must not collapse the two contexts into one generic user if that loses materially different success needs.
Must not invent interactive prompts or machine-readable formats.

cases.name: interrupted-delete-recovery
cases.trap: The scenario is happy-path-only or prescribes a confirmation modal/undo toast rather than describing the human situation, failure/edge condition, and observable recovery outcome.
cases.prompt: Create a Design Scenario from this accepted human-facing intent: a user managing personal tasks can accidentally delete a task and the accepted product capability allows recovery for at least 30 seconds in the same running session. Recovery restores the same task and displayed position and must not rewrite unrelated task history. The interface mechanism is deliberately open. Accepted authority does not define an exact recovery expiry after 30 seconds and does not promise cross-restart recovery; do not invent either. Produce the durable SC content.
expectations: Provides concrete context and a human goal around accidental deletion and regaining control, without assuming a particular modal/toast/button interaction.
Describes a human-visible journey/situation from deletion through noticing the mistake and attempting recovery within the guaranteed first 30 seconds of the same running session.

Includes a meaningful failure/interruption/edge condition that can affect the experience, such as distraction or interruption before recovery, while staying inside accepted authority and not inventing an exact recovery expiry or unsupported cross-restart behavior.

Defines the observable successful recovery outcome: restoration of the same task/position without rewriting unrelated task history. If the scenario discusses recovery outside the accepted same-session/minimum-window guarantee, it marks availability as unknown/conditional rather than inventing product semantics.
Keeps backend/storage mechanics out and traces the scenario to accepted human-facing authority.
negative_expectations: Must not require a confirmation dialog or undo toast as the only valid design.
Must not invent cross-restart or permanent-retention behavior.
Must not stop at a happy-path 'user deletes then restores task' narrative with no edge/failure condition.
Must not invent an exact recovery-expiry point merely to manufacture an unavailable-recovery state.

cases.name: deep-link-and-interruption-context
cases.trap: The scenario simply lists UI steps and ignores that the person arrives mid-flow with incomplete context and may be interrupted, so downstream design never has to solve orientation/re-entry.
cases.prompt: Create a Design Scenario for this accepted product need: an engineer receives a deep link in chat to a failed deployment while handling several incidents. Opening the link must let them determine which service failed and whether the failure still needs action. They may switch away and return several minutes later. The product already exposes deployment status/history, but navigation/layout are not fixed. Produce the durable SC content.
expectations: Makes the deep-link arrival and incident-pressure/multi-tasking context explicit because it materially affects orientation and continuity.
States the engineer's goal before interface steps: identify the failed service and whether action is still needed.
Describes a human-visible end-to-end situation without choosing a sidebar/page/modal structure.
Includes interruption/re-entry as a meaningful edge condition and requires the returning engineer to reconstruct current deployment context/status rather than relying on memory.
Defines observable outcome in terms of confidently identifying current failure/action state, not merely that a page loaded.
negative_expectations: Must not prescribe a particular page/sidebar/navigation component.
Must not omit interruption/re-entry despite it being part of the accepted context.
Must not define success as HTTP/page-load success.
